source_title: Steinhoff accounting scandal 2017 (named investigative journalism on the PwC forensic report; corroborated by company disclosures and JSE/Frankfurt market data)
publisher_issuer: Named journalism (amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism) reporting on the PwC forensic report; corroborated by company writedown disclosures
company_context: Steinhoff International was a global retail holding company with a primary listing on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and a secondary listing in Johannesburg, owning furniture and household-goods retail brands across Europe, Africa, the US and Australasia. In December 2017 CEO Markus Jooste resigned as accounting irregularities surfaced.
business_type: Multinational retail holding company (furniture / household goods)
macro_context: A serial-acquisition retail roll-up whose reported growth and asset values were inflated by fictitious and irregular transactions over nearly a decade; the unwinding triggered a near-total equity collapse and one of the largest corporate frauds in South African and European history.
evidence_summary: A PwC forensic investigation found that Steinhoff recorded fictitious or irregular transactions totalling approximately €6.5 billion (around $7.4 billion) between 2009 and 2017, inflating profit and asset values. CEO Markus Jooste resigned on 5 December 2017 just before the irregularities became public. In the first day after his resignation the shares fell about 58% on Frankfurt and 56% on Johannesburg; within two weeks they had lost almost 90% of their value. In 2018 Steinhoff announced roughly a $12 billion writedown reversing overstated revenues, profits and asset values. The company avoided immediate liquidation but underwent years of restructuring and litigation, with equity holders nearly wiped out.
owner_decision_context: Senior leadership, led by the CEO and close associates, allegedly orchestrated fictitious and irregular transactions to inflate reported profits and asset values over nearly a decade, so the board, auditors and investors relied on materially false financials until the scheme collapsed and immediate refinancing/restructuring became unavoidable.
action_taken: On disclosure the CEO resigned (5 Dec 2017); the company commissioned the PwC forensic investigation, restated accounts with a ~$12bn writedown, negotiated debt standstills and a multi-year restructuring with creditors, and entered prolonged litigation and a global settlement with shareholders.
outcome_evidence: Near-total equity collapse (almost 90% in two weeks), ~$12bn writedown, PwC finding of ~€6.5bn irregular transactions, and years of creditor restructuring confirm a fraud/governance-driven destruction of value rather than a market or operational downturn.
source_limitations: WebFetch typically 403s here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to named journalism (amaBhungane on the PwC report, BizNews, Moneyweb) and a Wikipedia summary citing company disclosures. The €6.5bn/$7.4bn figure is PwC's reported finding; the $12bn writedown is a company restatement figure. Final litigation/settlement totals are later events and excluded here.
directly_stated: CEO Markus Jooste resigned on 5 December 2017
Shares fell ~58% (Frankfurt) and ~56% (Johannesburg) on day one, almost 90% within two weeks
2018 writedown of approximately $12bn reversing overstated revenues, profits and asset values
inferred: Reported acquisition-driven growth and balance-sheet strength were substantially illusory, so conventional ratio analysis would have validated a false picture
The collapse was governance/control failure at the apex of the company, not an operating-market problem
why_useful_for_opsiq: Non-US, dual-listed large-cap fraud where a decade of fabricated transactions inflated both income statement and balance sheet. Tests whether the engine treats audited financials as potentially unreliable when governance red flags exist, classifies a fraud-driven value collapse, and triggers re-evaluation on new critical evidence (CEO resignation, forensic findings).
